newsitem.title: UK: Buoyant dlr ends just off two-year highs in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Buoyant dlr ends just off two-year highs in Europe.

text.p: The dollar closed firmer in Europe, just off fresh two year highs against the mark, the Swiss franc and the French currency as dealers braced themselves for further evidence of buoyant economic growth in the U.S.

The firm dollar tone was helped by another assault on the mark on its European crosses. The spectacular rise of the Norwegian crown continued, pushing the mark below 4.00 crowns for the first time since September 1992.
"The dollar rally is all about interest rate rise speculation in the U.S. and rate cut expectations in Europe," said Ian Harwood, head of strategy and economics at Kleinwort Benson.
"The key to the dollar rally is the gloom about European growth, and I can't really see it lifting," said Harwood.

At 1540 GMT the dollar was at 1.5868/76 marks, off a 29-month high at 1.5890 and up from 1.5852/57 in late Europe on Friday. Against the yen, it was at 116.29, up from 115.96/116.00 at the previous European close.

The U.S. unit set a fresh 31-month high against the Swiss franc at 1.3796 per dollar and rose to a new two-year high at 5.3605 French francs before settling back to 1.3763/69 and 5.3530/50 respectively in late trade. Mark/Norwegian crown was at 4.0055/85 after dropping as low as 3.9988.
U.S. December jobs data released last Friday helped fuel rate rise expectations. Non-farm payrolls rose by 262,000 against average expecations for a rise of about 200,000.
An monthly increase of 0.5 percent in average hourly earnings set inflation alarm bells ringing.
The U.S. jobs data were in clear contrast to German unemployment figures, also released last week, which showed another marked rise by 48,000 to 4.156 milion, or 10.8 percent of the workforce.
A slowdown in GDP growth also fueled gloomy views about Germany's economic prospects.

"The key thing is the market's got a much more realistic view of economic prospects this year in Germany and hence, there are increased expectations of a German rate cut," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
Further clues about interest rate prospects will be gleaned from U.S. inflation data on Tuesday.
Economists polled by Reuters expect the CPI to have risen by 0.3 percent last month, with core prices up 0.2 percent.
"If the figure exceeds expectations, there is a risk that this will disturb the bond markets and therefore weigh on the dollar," said Harwood at Kleinwort Benson.
"But it looks more likely that the dollar will go higher based on favourable interest rate differentials," he said.
Even a higher-than-expected CPI was unlikely to prompt the Federal Reserve into tightening credit at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting on February 4-5, said Harwood.
U.S. December retail sales, also due on Tuesday, are expected to gain 0.5 percent, after a 0.4-percent drop in November. Industrial production data are also due on Friday.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said after the G10 meeting in Basle the G10 was not concerned about exchange rates within Europe or between Europe and the U.S.
He said G10 central bank governors had no reason for specific concerns in the area of European and dollar exchange rates.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, meanwhile, reiterated his support for a strong dollar, saying a strong U.S. currency was in the country's economic interest.

Dollar/yen also firmed as fears of Japanese capital repatriation in the wake of the slump of Japan's stockmarket receded. But dealers said concern that Japan might not want to see a much weaker yen kept dollar/yen under wraps.
-- Astrid Zweynert London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792
